title: よーい、アクション  (Lights, Camera, Action)

segments.t: Welcome to episode one of The Naked Director, or Zenra Kantoku in Japanese. We open in a bright Tokyo studio before jumping back to where Toru Muranishi started. Kaoru Kuroki speaks politely about living naturally and about love, while Muranishi gets his camera ready to roll. Just listen to the rhythm first without worrying about every detail.
わたくしは日本の風潮に問題があると思っております。
日本には恥じらいの文化がございます。
それに縛られる必要はございません。
でも恥ずかしいなんて思いませんよ。
あるがままに生きることが人間らしさです。
わたくしのテーマは愛でございます。
そして愛とは自然の受容でございます。
ありがとうございます。
皆さんにミラクルが起きる瞬間をお見せします。
目を閉じないでください。
いいですね？それでは参ります。
よーい、アクション！
Kuroki speaks with extra-polished studio manners, while Muranishi addresses the room like a showman. Let's hear their key lines up close.
わたくしは日本の風潮に問題があると思っております。

'I believe there is a problem with current attitudes in Japan.' Kuroki refers to herself as "watakushi", a dressed-up cousin of everyday "watashi". Inside her sentence, "mondai" means problem, followed by "ga aru", there is.
日本には恥じらいの文化がございます。

'In Japan, there is a culture of shyness.' Starting with "Nihon ni wa" sets Japan up as the place we are talking about. At the end, "gozaimasu" is the extra-polite twin of "arimasu", meaning something exists.
それに縛られる必要はございません。

'There is no need to be bound by that.' Listen for "hitsuyou", need, paired with "gozaimasen", the negative form that says none exists. Put any action before "hitsuyou wa nai" or "hitsuyou wa arimasen" to say you do not need to do it.
でも恥ずかしいなんて思いませんよ。

'Still, I do not feel embarrassed at all.' Opening with "demo" pivots straight into 'but'. "Hazukashii" means embarrassed or shy, and ending on "omoidasen"—here "omoimasen yo"—adds a confident "yo" to press the point home.
あるがままに生きることが人間らしさです。

'Living just as you are is what makes us human.' "Arugamama" paints the picture of things exactly as they are, built around "aru", to be, and "ikiru" means to live. Adding "rashisa" onto "ningen", human being, turns 'human' into 'human-ness'.
わたくしのテーマは愛でございます。
'My theme is love.' Borrowed from German, "teema" is the everyday word for theme. After "wa", she names "ai", love, and wraps up with "de gozaimasu", a grander, stage-worthy way to say "desu".
ありがとうございます。
'Thank you very much.' You will hear "arigatou gozaimasu" everywhere in daily life, from shops to television sets. Dropping "gozaimasu" leaves casual "arigatou" for friends and family.
皆さんにミラクルが起きる瞬間をお見せします。

'I will show everyone the moment a miracle happens.' "Minasan" addresses everyone in the room respectfully, built from "mina", all, plus polite "san". "Shunkan" is an instant or split second, and "omise shimasu" humbles the speaker while promising to show something.
目を閉じないでください。

'Please do not close your eyes.' "Me" is eye or eyes—Japanese leaves out any separate word for 'your' when body parts are obvious. Attach "nai de kudasai" to "tojiru", to shut, whenever you want to say 'please do not'.
いいですね？
'Are you ready?' Literally "ii desu ne" asks 'is it good, right?', checking that everyone is following along. A rising tone turns that short check into 'ready?' or 'got it?'.
よーい、アクション！

'Ready, action!' Directors on Japanese sets stretch out "yooi", meaning preparation or 'get set', right before calling borrowed English "akushon". Now let's listen to the whole studio opening again from start to finish.
わたくしは日本の風潮に問題があると思っております。
日本には恥じらいの文化がございます。
それに縛られる必要はございません。
でも恥ずかしいなんて思いませんよ。
あるがままに生きることが人間らしさです。
わたくしのテーマは愛でございます。
そして愛とは自然の受容でございます。
ありがとうございます。
皆さんにミラクルが起きる瞬間をお見せします。
目を閉じないでください。
いいですね？それでは参ります。
よーい、アクション！

Notice how "watakushi" and "gozaimasu" instantly give Japanese speech a formal, public polish, while "nai de kudasai" gives you a clean, polite way to ask someone not to do something. Until next scene—see you again.
また会いましょう。
